acid-base-titrations-s1.title: Titration of an unknown acid
acid-base-titrations-s1.text: A student titrates 25.00 mL of a monoprotic weak acid, HA, of unknown concentration with 0.100 M NaOH, recording the pH with a calibrated meter. The steepest rise is centered at 20.00 mL.

acid-base-titrations-s2.title: Four snapshots of a titration
acid-base-titrations-s2.html: Key: HA weak acid molecule; A⁻ its conjugate base; Na⁺ sodium ion; OH⁻ hydroxide. Water and the very few H₃O⁺ and OH⁻ ions made by the equilibria are not drawn. All four boxes come from the same titration, at different volumes of NaOH.

acid-base-titrations-s3.title: Two acids, one base
acid-base-titrations-s3.text: 25.0 mL of 0.100 M HCl and 25.0 mL of 0.100 M acetic acid (Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵) are each titrated with 0.100 M NaOH.

acid-base-titrations-s4.title: Titrating a weak base
acid-base-titrations-s4.text: 25.0 mL of 0.100 M aqueous ammonia, NH₃ (Kb = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵), is titrated with 0.100 M HCl.

acid-base-titrations-s5.title: A titration with two steep rises
acid-base-titrations-s5.text: 20.0 mL of 0.100 M of an acid, H₂A, is titrated with 0.100 M NaOH.

items.q: What is the concentration of HA in the original solution? Include the unit.

mistakes.why: Value: you used the last volume on the graph. Use the equivalence volume, at the center of the steep rise: 20.00 mL.
Value: 10.00 mL is the half-equivalence point. The moles of base equal the moles of acid at 20.00 mL.

why.correct: At equivalence, mol OH⁻ = mol HA: 0.02000 L × 0.100 mol/L = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol. [HA] = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol / 0.02500 L = 0.0800 M.

items.q: Which reading from the curve gives the pKa of HA?
options: The pH at 10.00 mL, 4.20
The pH at 20.00 mL, 8.42
The pH at 0 mL, 2.65
The pH at 30.00 mL, 12.26

why.correct: At the half-equivalence point (half of 20.00 mL), half the HA has become A⁻, so [HA] = [A⁻]. In Ka = [H₃O⁺][A⁻]/[HA] the two cancel: Ka = [H₃O⁺], so pH = pKa.
options: Right: half-equivalence, where [HA] = [A⁻].
This is the equivalence point, where no HA is left; its pH is set by A⁻ acting as a base. Confusing equivalence with half-equivalence is the most common titration error.
At the start no A⁻ has been made, so [HA] ≠ [A⁻].
Past equivalence the pH is set by excess OH⁻.

items.q: Use the curve to find Ka of HA. Give your answer in scientific notation.

mistakes.why: Value: you used the pH at the equivalence point. Read the pH at half the equivalence volume (10.00 mL), where pH = pKa.

items.q: Calculate the pH at the equivalence point. (Use Ka = 6.3 × 10⁻⁵.)

mistakes.why: Value: pH 7.00 is the equivalence point only for a strong acid with a strong base. Here A⁻, a weak base, is left.
Value: the volume is now 45.00 mL, so [A⁻] = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol / 0.04500 L = 0.0444 M.
Value: that is the pOH. Subtract from 14.00.

items.q: A second student repeats the titration with 25.00 mL of the same acid diluted to 50.00 mL with water first. Which change to the curve is expected?
options: The equivalence point stays at 20.00 mL, and the pH at 10.00 mL stays about the same
The equivalence point moves to 40.00 mL, because the volume doubled
The equivalence point moves to 10.00 mL, because the acid is more dilute
The pH at 10.00 mL drops, because there is more water to ionize

why.correct: Adding water does not change the moles of HA, so the same 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol of OH⁻ (20.00 mL) reaches equivalence. At half-equivalence [HA] = [A⁻] still, so pH = pKa again.
options: Right: moles of acid set the equivalence volume; the ratio at half-equivalence is unchanged.
The equivalence volume depends on moles of acid, not on the volume the acid is dissolved in.
The moles of acid are the same, so the base needed is the same.
pH = pKa at half-equivalence whatever the dilution, because [HA]/[A⁻] = 1.

items.q: Which box shows the solution at the equivalence point?
options: Z
W
X
Y

why.correct: At equivalence, base added equals acid present: all 6 HA became 6 A⁻, with 6 Na⁺ from the 6 NaOH, and no OH⁻ left over.
options: Right: only A⁻ and Na⁺.
Box W is the half-equivalence point: half the HA has been converted.
Box X is the start: no base added yet.
Box Y is past equivalence: 2 extra OH⁻.

items.q: At which box does pH = pKa of HA?
options: W
Z
X
Y

why.correct: [HA] = [A⁻] (3 and 3), so in Ka = [H₃O⁺][A⁻]/[HA] the ratio is 1 and [H₃O⁺] = Ka.
options: Right: equal amounts of the acid and its conjugate base.
Box Z has no HA left; it is the equivalence point, not the half-equivalence point.
At the start there is no A⁻, so the ratio is not 1.
Past equivalence, excess OH⁻ sets the pH.

items.q: Put the boxes in the order they occur during the titration.
options: X
W
Z
Y

why.correct: Start (only HA), half-equivalence (equal HA and A⁻), equivalence (only A⁻), then past equivalence (A⁻ plus excess OH⁻). Na⁺ rises as NaOH is added: 0, 3, 6, 8.

items.q: Which statement about Box Z is correct?
options: Its pH is above 7, because A⁻ takes protons from water
Its pH is 7, because equal moles of acid and base have reacted
Its pH equals pKa, because no HA remains
Its pH is below 7, because HA was the starting acid

why.correct: A⁻ is a weak base: A⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HA + OH⁻. With no HA or strong acid left, that small amount of OH⁻ makes the solution basic.
options: Right: the conjugate base of a weak acid gives a basic equivalence point.
Equal moles give pH 7 only for strong acid with strong base.
pH = pKa needs equal HA and A⁻; Z has no HA.
All the HA has been converted; the acid is gone.

items.q: Suppose each particle drawn stands for 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol, the NaOH is 0.100 M, and the HA has pKa 4.74. How many mL of NaOH had been added at Box Y?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the equivalence volume. Box Y has 8 Na⁺, so 8 NaOH units were added.
Value: count the Na⁺ ions, not the excess OH⁻: each NaOH added one Na⁺.

why.correct: Na⁺ counts the NaOH added: 8 × 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol = 4.00 × 10⁻³ mol. Volume = 4.00 × 10⁻³ mol ÷ 0.100 mol/L = 0.0400 L = 40.0 mL. (The pKa is not needed.)

items.q: Which curve belongs to acetic acid, and what shows it?
options: Acid 2: it starts at a higher pH and its equivalence point is above pH 7
Acid 1: it starts at a lower pH, so it has fewer H₃O⁺ ions
Acid 2: it needs more NaOH to reach equivalence
Acid 1: its equivalence point is at pH 7, which shows a partly ionized acid

why.correct: Acetic acid is mostly un-ionized, so its starting pH (2.88) is higher than HCl's (1.00), and at equivalence acetate makes the solution basic (pH 8.72).
options: Right: higher start, basic equivalence point.
A lower pH means more H₃O⁺, not fewer; Acid 1 is the strong acid.
Both need 25.0 mL: equal moles of acid need equal moles of base, whatever their strength.
pH 7 at equivalence is the mark of a strong acid with a strong base.

items.q: Why do both acids reach equivalence at the same volume of NaOH?
options: They contain the same moles of acid, and OH⁻ reacts with each to completion
They have the same pH at the start
Both acids ionize fully once NaOH is added
The NaOH is a strong base, so it reaches equivalence at 25.0 mL with any acid

why.correct: Each flask holds 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol of acid. OH⁻ removes HCl's H₃O⁺ and also takes the proton from acetic acid molecules directly (K = 1.8 × 10⁹), so each needs 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol OH⁻.
options: Right: equivalence counts total acid, ionized or not.
Their starting pH values differ by almost two units.
Before equivalence, acetic acid is still mostly molecules; what matters is that OH⁻ reacts with those molecules.
The equivalence volume depends on the moles of acid present, not only on the base.

items.q: Calculate the pH of the HCl flask after 10.0 mL of NaOH has been added.

mistakes.why: Value: divide by the total volume, 35.0 mL, not the 25.0 mL of acid.
Value: that is the starting pH. Subtract the 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol OH⁻ added first.

items.q: Calculate the pH of the acetic acid flask after 10.0 mL of NaOH has been added.

mistakes.why: Value: that treats acetic acid as strong. After the reaction you have a mixture of CH₃COOH and CH₃COO⁻: use [H₃O⁺] = Ka × [HA]/[A⁻].
Value: the ratio is upside down. [H₃O⁺] = Ka × [HA]/[A⁻] = Ka × 1.50/1.00.

why.correct: OH⁻ converts 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol acid to acetate, leaving 1.50 × 10⁻³ mol CH₃COOH. [H₃O⁺] = Ka × [HA]/[A⁻] = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ × 1.50/1.00 = 2.7 × 10⁻⁵ M; pH = 4.57.

items.q: The acetic acid titration is repeated with 25.0 mL of 0.200 M acetic acid (same 0.100 M NaOH). Predict the change in each.

variables.name: Volume of NaOH at the equivalence point
variables.why: Twice the moles of acid need twice the moles of OH⁻: 50.0 mL.

variables.name: pH at the half-equivalence point
variables.why: At half-equivalence [HA] = [A⁻] for any starting amount, so pH = pKa = 4.74 again.

variables.name: Starting pH
variables.why: A more concentrated weak acid makes more H₃O⁺: √(Ka·C) grows with C.

why.correct: The equivalence volume tracks the moles of acid; the half-equivalence pH tracks the acid itself.

items.q: What is the pH at 12.5 mL of HCl (half-equivalence), and what does it equal?
options: 9.26, the pKa of NH₄⁺
4.74, the pKb of NH₃
5.28, the pKa of NH₄⁺
7.00, because half the base is neutralized

why.correct: At half-equivalence [NH₃] = [NH₄⁺]. For the acid of this pair, Ka = [H₃O⁺][NH₃]/[NH₄⁺] = [H₃O⁺], so pH = pKa of NH₄⁺ = 14.00 − pKb = 9.26.
options: Right: half-equivalence gives pKa of the conjugate acid.
pKb is the pOH at half-equivalence, not the pH. Using pKb where pKa of the conjugate acid belongs is a frequent error with weak bases.
That is the pH at equivalence, 25.0 mL.
Half-neutralized ammonia is a basic mixture of NH₃ and NH₄⁺, not a neutral one.

items.q: Calculate the pH at the equivalence point.

mistakes.why: Value: NH₄⁺, the conjugate acid of a weak base, is left at equivalence, so the pH is below 7.
Value: the volume doubled to 50.0 mL, so [NH₄⁺] = 0.0500 M.
Value: you used Kb. NH₄⁺ is an acid: Ka = Kw/Kb = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰.

items.q: Apart from water and Cl⁻, which species is present in the greatest amount at 25.0 mL?
options: NH₄⁺
NH₃
H₃O⁺
OH⁻

why.correct: At equivalence every NH₃ has been converted to NH₄⁺. A small fraction of NH₄⁺ gives a proton to water, which is why the pH is below 7.
options: Right: the conjugate acid is what remains.
Only a trace of NH₃ re-forms from NH₄⁺.
H₃O⁺ is about 5 × 10⁻⁶ M, far below the 0.0500 M NH₄⁺.
The solution is acidic, so OH⁻ is scarce.

items.q: How does this curve differ from the acetic acid curve in the previous set, and why?
options: It falls instead of rising, because acid is added to a base; its equivalence pH is below 7
It rises like the acetic acid curve, because both titrations end with excess titrant
It has the same equivalence pH, because Ka of acetic acid equals Kb of ammonia
It falls, because ammonia is a strong base

why.correct: Adding HCl lowers the pH, so the curve runs downhill. The equivalence point holds NH₄⁺, a weak acid, so its pH is about 5.3, a mirror of acetate's 8.7.
options: Right: downhill, with an acidic equivalence point.
Excess HCl makes the end of this curve acidic, not basic: the curve goes down.
The two K values match, but one equivalence point holds a weak acid (NH₄⁺) and the other a weak base (CH₃COO⁻).
Ammonia is a weak base, which is why the curve has a buffer region and an acidic equivalence point.

items.q: What do the two steep rises, at 20.0 mL and 40.0 mL, show?
options: H₂A gives up two protons, one at a time
The solution contains two different acids
The NaOH ran out halfway and was refilled
The first rise is the half-equivalence point and the second the equivalence point

why.correct: A diprotic acid has one equivalence point per proton: H₂A → HA⁻ (first 20.0 mL), then HA⁻ → A²⁻ (next 20.0 mL). Equal volumes, because each step removes the same moles of protons.
options: Right: one equivalence point per ionizable proton.
Two acids could also give two rises, but the equal 20.0 mL steps fit one diprotic acid with 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol of each proton.
A titration curve plots the pH of the flask; refilling a buret does not show up.
A half-equivalence point lies in a flat buffer region, not at a steep rise.

items.q: Which reading gives pKa₂, the pKa of HA⁻?
options: pH at 30.0 mL, 8.50
pH at 10.0 mL, 4.00
pH at 20.0 mL, 6.25

why.correct: Between the first equivalence point (20.0 mL) and the second (40.0 mL), OH⁻ converts HA⁻ to A²⁻. Halfway, at 30.0 mL, [HA⁻] = [A²⁻], so pH = pKa₂.
options: Right: the second half-equivalence point.
That is the second equivalence point, where all HA⁻ has become A²⁻.
That is pKa₁, halfway to the first equivalence point.
That is the first equivalence point, where HA⁻ is the main species.

items.q: Apart from Na⁺ and water, which species is present in the greatest amount at 20.0 mL?
options: HA⁻
H₂A
A²⁻
OH⁻

why.correct: At the first equivalence point exactly one proton per H₂A has been removed: all 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol H₂A has become HA⁻.
options: Right: the first equivalence point holds HA⁻.
H₂A is used up at the first equivalence point.
A²⁻ forms only after 20.0 mL.
No excess OH⁻ is present until after 40.0 mL.

items.q: Which statements are supported by the curve? Select all that apply.
options: pKa₁ of H₂A is about 4.0
Ka₂ is larger than Ka₁
Three times as much NaOH is needed to reach the second equivalence point as the first
At 10.0 mL, [H₂A] is about equal to [HA⁻]
H₂A is a strong acid

why.correct: At 10.0 mL (first half-equivalence) [H₂A] ≈ [HA⁻] and pH ≈ pKa₁ = 4.0; the second equivalence point is at 40.0 mL, twice (not three times) 20.0 mL.
options: Right: read at 10.0 mL.
pKa₂ (8.5) is larger than pKa₁ (4.0), so Ka₂ is smaller: the second proton comes off a negative ion and is held more tightly.
40.0 mL is twice 20.0 mL: each proton needs the same moles of OH⁻, so the second equivalence point needs twice the NaOH of the first.
Right: half of H₂A converted to HA⁻.
A strong acid would start near pH 1.0 and show no flat region before the first rise.

items.q: For a weak acid titrated with NaOH, put the regions of the curve in order and match each to what sets its pH.
options: Start: the weak acid alone (Ka equilibrium)
Before equivalence: HA and A⁻ together, [H₃O⁺] = Ka × [HA]/[A⁻]
Half-equivalence: [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa
Equivalence: A⁻ alone (Kb = Kw/Ka), pH above 7
After equivalence: excess OH⁻

why.correct: Each region has one equilibrium that controls it. Find which species are left after the neutralization, then pick the matching method.

items.q: A 25.00 mL sample of 0.1200 M HNO₂ is titrated with 0.1500 M KOH. What volume of KOH reaches the equivalence point?

mistakes.why: Value: you inverted the ratio of concentrations. V(KOH) = mol HNO₂ / M(KOH) = (0.02500 L × 0.1200 M) / 0.1500 M.

items.q: Before filling a buret with NaOH titrant, a student rinses it with distilled water and does not rinse it with the NaOH. How does this affect the calculated concentration of the acid?
options: Too high, because the diluted NaOH needs a larger volume to reach equivalence
Too low, because the NaOH is diluted
No effect, because water is neutral
Too low, because less NaOH is needed

why.correct: Water left in the buret dilutes the NaOH, so more volume is delivered to supply the same moles of OH⁻. The student multiplies that larger volume by the labelled molarity and overestimates the acid.
options: Right: larger volume × assumed molarity = too many moles.
The NaOH is diluted, but the calculation uses the labelled molarity, so the error runs the other way.
Water does not change the moles of acid, but it lowers the molarity of the titrant actually used.
Diluted titrant means more volume is needed, not less.

items.q: A student claims, "At the equivalence point of any titration, the pH is 7." Which evidence best refutes the claim?
options: A titration of 0.10 M NH₃ with HCl reaches equivalence near pH 5
A titration of 0.10 M HCl with NaOH reaches equivalence at pH 7.00
Equivalence is reached when moles of titrant equal moles of analyte
The steep rise in a titration curve is centered on the equivalence point

why.correct: One counterexample refutes "any". At the equivalence point of NH₃ with HCl, the flask holds NH₄⁺, a weak acid, so the pH is below 7.
options: Right: a concrete case with a non-7 equivalence pH.
This case agrees with the claim, so it cannot refute it.
True, but it says nothing about the pH.
True, but it does not say what that pH is.

items.q: On a titration curve of a weak acid with NaOH, the steep rise is centered at 32.40 mL. At what volume of NaOH does pH = pKa?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the equivalence volume. pH = pKa at half of it, where [HA] = [A⁻].
Value: pH = pKa comes before the equivalence point, at half its volume, not double.

why.correct: Half-equivalence is half the equivalence volume: 32.40 mL ÷ 2 = 16.20 mL. There half the acid has become A⁻, so [HA] = [A⁻] and pH = pKa.
